extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, psychology, and education; readers interested in scientific method applied to human nature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for investigating and explaining the formation of character (ethology) using principles of scientific method — distinguishing empirical laws from causal laws and deciding when to use deduction, induction, or observation. Targets methodological standards for studying complex human phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an Empirical Law
rubrics_metrics.description: An Empirical Law is a uniformity, whether of succession or of co-existence, which holds true in all instances within our limits of observation, but is not of a nature to afford any assurance that it would hold beyond those limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical laws may be true in observed cases yet depend on prior causes not ascertained, or be resolvable into simpler sequences and thus exposed to many possibilities of counteraction. Therefore, when using empirical laws one must ask 'why is it true?' and beware applying it outside observed time/place/circumstance (examples: 'all men are liars' in certain ages; caution about applying maxims collected from one nation to another).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific truths are causal laws, not mere empirical generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: The really scientific truths are not empirical laws but the causal laws which explain them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical laws serve to verify the conclusions of theory; scientific understanding requires resolving empirical regularities into the causal laws that produce them. Without such causal explanation, empirical generalizations are only approximate and unreliable for extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical laws are approximate for complex phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: In complex subjects (e.g., human conduct), empirical laws are only approximate generalizations because innumerable circumstances influence effects even if the underlying causal laws are few and simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in 'simpler' sciences like astronomy, direct observation yields only approximations (planets don't move in exact ellipses). Expect greater approximation and less universality in moral/complex sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Deductive Method for the formation of character (Ethology)
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of the formation of character are to be obtained by deduction from the general laws of mind (Psychology); Ethology, the science of character, is essentially deductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because character and its formative circumstances are highly complex and not amenable to controlled experiment or exhaustive observation, one should deduce how general psychological laws will operate under assumed sets of circumstances rather than attempt direct experimental production of character (practical obstacles to experimental control and recording are cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of experimental and observational inquiry in studying character
rubrics_metrics.description: It is practically impossible to perform experiments or observations with the completeness needed to determine the causes forming character (e.g., to bring up many humans from infancy while recording every impression).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One trivial overlooked circumstance can vitiate a purportedly controlled experiment. Observational study is likewise limited: we can rarely ascertain an individual's character completely, and a single action or short conduct provides little evidence. Hence direct experiment/observation yields only rough, aggregate, or comparative results requiring large numbers to eliminate chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve empirical laws into their causal conditions before extrapolating
rubrics_metrics.description: Before applying empirical maxims beyond their observed domain, we must resolve them into the laws of the causes on which they depend and ascertain that those causes extend to the new case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If we can connect observed differences (e.g., national or sex differences) to general causal laws (government, education, social conditions, bodily differences), then observation can verify deduction; otherwise empirical generalizations are unreliable as presumptions for unfamiliar cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethology: definition and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethology (the Science of Character) is the deductive science which determines the kind of character produced by any set of circumstances, physical and moral, from the general laws of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethology corresponds to the art of education broadly, including formation of national or collective character. Its propositions are hypothetical and assert tendencies rather than certainties; they indicate what tends to occur when causes operate uncounteracted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate scientific propositions as tendencies, not certainties
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific propositions in Ethology must be hypothetical only, and affirm tendencies, not facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements should assert that a given cause 'tends' to produce an effect (e.g., 'bodily strength tends to make men courageous') rather than asserting it always does. This acknowledges the possibility of counteracting influences while retaining universal validity of the tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and acquisition of middle principles (axiomata media)
rubrics_metrics.description: The middle principles (axiomata media) of a science principally constitute its value; they lie between lowest empirical generalizations and highest general laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should obtain principles in the order in which real induction is practicable. Poincaré criticizes Bacon's rigid insistence on ascending from lowest to middle to highest; in many sciences the highest generalizations were ascertained early and then used deductively. The practical maxim is: obtain those truths first for which conditions of real induction can most completely be realized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simplest cases (fewest causes) for induction to derive general laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Where our means of investigation can reach causes, the simplest cases, involving the fewest causes, are most amenable to inductive process and elicit laws of greatest comprehensiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In every science that reaches causes, begin with simple cases to deduce broad laws, then derive middle principles; complex cases are built from these simpler causal laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification: compare deductions against empirical generalizations, not isolated instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Before relying on deductions, verify them by comparison with empirical generalizations collected from many instances rather than by single instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The verification step should confront deductions with the aggregated empirical laws (examples: Newton verifying by deducing Kepler's laws rather than individual planetary positions). This reduces susceptibility to accidental coincidences in single observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational inference requires numerous and representative instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions from observation alone deserve no reliance unless instances are numerous enough to eliminate chance and every assignable circumstance in which cases may resemble one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative claims about national or class character require sufficiently large and fairly selected samples; small or nonrepresentative observation yields only rough comparative results and not genuine induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating perceived mental differences as ultimate facts; seek outward causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not dogmatically assume mental differences are ultimate and inexplicable; instead attempt to refer them to outward causes (education, circumstances, bodily organization) by analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many mental differences are consequences of prior mental history or physical organization and can be explained by general laws of association (example: synchronous vs successive sensations produce different cognitive styles — perceptive vs ratiocinative). Failure to seek such explanations is unscientific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for organic (physiological) contributions without overattribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that organic differences in bodily structure may contribute to mental predispositions, but do not assume direct or exclusive causation without analysis; many effects occur via altered sensations which then operate through mental laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organic differences may intensify sensations, which then produce stronger associative or affective responses; instincts may have a more direct organic link, but even instincts are modifiable by education. Recent cerebral physiology rejects crude phrenology; investigations should seek precise kinds of connections.
